envelope.sourceCitation: 14 CFR 67.103(c), 67.203(c), 67.303(c); AME Guide Item 52, Color Vision Screening Steps; AME Guide, Acceptable Color Vision Tests for Pilots; FAA Color Vision FAQs (Updated 08/27/2025); Medical Certificate Limitations (Updated 12/12/2024); FAA Color Vision flowchart (Updated 09/24/2025)

body:
The color vision standard is the same for all three classes. Under 14 CFR 67.103(c), 67.203(c) and 67.303(c), the standard is the "Ability to perceive those colors necessary for the safe performance of airman duties."

How the FAA tests it changed on January 1, 2025. The FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners (Item 52) states: "Testing frequency will change to a one-time color vision deficiency screening." The FAA's acceptable tests page for pilots states: "Testing must be performed in person. Virtual testing, downloaded, or printed versions of color vision tests are prohibited." The tests it lists are the Colour Assessment & Diagnosis (CAD) test, the Rabin Cone Test (RCCT) and the Waggoner Computerized Color Vision Test.

Who is tested. The FAA Color Vision FAQs (Updated 08/27/2025) state: "The AME only needs to test NEW pilots, those with a limitation 16 or 17 who want it removed, or those with a current LOE or SODA who want to upgrade." Item 52 separately covers "a returning pilot who historically passed any previously FAA-approved color vision test" and says that for all classes, a computer-based screening test is not required.

If a first-time applicant cannot pass any of the acceptable tests, Item 52 instructs the AME to "ISSUE a 3rd Class medical certificate (if otherwise qualified)" and to add limitation #104, which reads "Valid for day visual flight rules (VFR) only." It continues: "If the individual requests an upgrade to 1st or 2nd class, they should appeal to the Federal Air Surgeon."

A pilot who already holds a color vision SODA or Letter of Evidence (LOE) is handled differently. For a 3rd class SODA or LOE holder who wants to keep 3rd class, Item 52 states: "Does not need computer test. Issue 3rd class certificate with no color vision limitation (if otherwise qualified)." For a pilot who holds a 1st or 2nd class LOE or SODA, it states: "Does not need computer test." The FAQs add: "Whatever the individual has walking into the AME's office (e.g., LOE, restricted certificate/any class, unrestricted, failed) is what they will walk out with, unless they take a new color test."

A third-class SODA or LOE holder who takes a 2025 computer test to upgrade and does not pass: Item 52 screening steps (page last updated 08/27/2025) say issue limitation #104. The color vision flowchart dated 09/24/2025 says keep the previous limitation. The FAA pages differ. Confirm with your AME which instruction they are using.

For what a SODA is, see the Statement of Demonstrated Ability (SODA) record.

links.title: AME Guide Item 52: Color Vision Screening Steps
AME Guide: Acceptable Color Vision Tests for Pilots

cardTitle: Hearing - three ways to meet the standard
body:
The hearing standard is identical for all three classes of medical certificate, and it offers three alternatives. Under 14 CFR 67.105(a) (first class), 67.205(a) (second class) and 67.305(a) (third class), "The person shall demonstrate acceptable hearing by at least one of the following tests".

The first is a conversational voice test: "Demonstrate an ability to hear an average conversational voice in a quiet room, using both ears, at a distance of 6 feet from the examiner, with the back turned to the examiner."

The second is speech discrimination: "Demonstrate an acceptable understanding of speech as determined by audiometric speech discrimination testing to a score of at least 70 percent obtained in one ear or in a sound field environment."

The third is pure tone audiometry, measured against a table of worst acceptable thresholds. At 500, 1000, 2000 and 3000 Hz the better ear may not exceed 35, 30, 30 and 40 dB, and the poorer ear may not exceed 35, 50, 50 and 60 dB. These figures are identical across all three classes.

Meeting any one of the three satisfies the standard. The same sections also require no disease or condition of the middle or internal ear, nose, oral cavity, pharynx or larynx that interferes with, or is aggravated by, flying, or that interferes with clear and effective speech communication, and no condition manifested by vertigo or a disturbance of equilibrium.

links.title: 14 CFR 67.105 - Ear, nose, throat, and equilibrium (first class)
14 CFR 67.305 - Ear, nose, throat, and equilibrium (third class)

envelope.sourceCitation: 14 CFR 67.401(a), (b), (d), (f), (i); FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, Statement of Demonstrated Ability (SODA) and Items 23-24

body:
Under 14 CFR 67.401(b), "At the discretion of the Federal Air Surgeon, a Statement of Demonstrated Ability (SODA) may be granted, instead of an Authorization, to a person whose disqualifying condition is static or nonprogressive and who has been found capable of performing airman duties without endangering public safety. A SODA does not expire and authorizes a designated aviation medical examiner to issue a medical certificate of a specified class if the examiner finds that the condition described on its face has not adversely changed."

The SODA names the class. Under 14 CFR 67.401(d), "In granting an Authorization or SODA under this section, the Federal Air Surgeon specifies the class of medical certificate authorized to be issued". The FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners (Items 23-24) states: "The Examiner must take special care not to issue a medical certificate of a higher class than that specified on the face of the SODA even if the applicant appears to be otherwise medically qualified."

A SODA does not expire, but it can be withdrawn. Under 14 CFR 67.401(f), "An Authorization or SODA granted under the provisions of this section to a person who does not meet the applicable provisions of subparts B, C, or D of this part may be withdrawn, at the discretion of the Federal Air Surgeon, at any time if" (1) "There is adverse change in the holder's medical condition"; (2) "The holder fails to comply with a statement of functional limitations or operational limitations issued as a condition of certification under this section"; (3) "Public safety would be endangered by the holder's exercise of airman privileges"; (4) "The holder fails to provide medical information reasonably needed by the Federal Air Surgeon for certification under this section"; or (5) "The holder makes or causes to be made a statement that is the basis for withdrawal of an Authorization, including a SODA, under subpart D of part 3 of this chapter."

If that happens, 14 CFR 67.401(i) sets out the procedure. The holder "will be served a letter of withdrawal, stating the reason for the action." Then, "By not later than 60 days after the service of the letter of withdrawal, the holder of the Authorization or SODA may request, in writing, that the Federal Air Surgeon provide for review of the decision to withdraw. The request for review may be accompanied by supporting medical evidence." A written final decision affirming or reversing the withdrawal is issued "Within 60 days of receipt of a request for review". A medical certificate rendered invalid by a withdrawal "shall be surrendered to the Administrator upon request."

An Authorization is different on the point of time. Under 14 CFR 67.401(a), an Authorization is "valid for a specified period".

Color vision is handled separately. See the FAA color vision testing (2025) record.

AME Guide: Items 23-24, SODA and SODA Serial Number

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners - CACI Conditions

body:
CACI stands for Conditions AMEs Can Issue. The FAA describes it this way: "Conditions AMEs Can Issue (CACI) is a series of conditions which allow AMEs to regular issue if the applicant meets the parameters of the CACI Condition Worksheet. The worksheets provide detailed instructions to the examiner and outline condition-specific requirements for the applicant."

The practical consequence is that a CACI condition does not automatically mean a Special Issuance. The FAA states that "If all the CACI criteria are met and the applicant is otherwise qualified, the AME may issue on the first exam or the first time the condition is reported to the AME without contacting AMCD/RFS."

Your supporting documents stay with the examiner in that case. The FAA instructs the AME to "Document the appropriate notes in Block 60 and keep the supporting documents in your files; they do not need to be submitted to the FAA at this time."

If the criteria are not met, the path changes: "If the requirements are not met, the AME must defer the exam and send the supporting documents to the FAA."

The FAA also directs the examiner to "Review the disposition table BEFORE the CACI worksheet to verify a CACI is required." There are 29 published CACI condition worksheets.

links.title: FAA Guide for AMEs - CACI Conditions and worksheets

envelope.sourceCitation: 14 CFR 67.407, 14 CFR 67.409; FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners - CACI Conditions

cardTitle: Deferred or denied - what each one means
body:
Deferral and denial are not the same thing, and only one of them starts a clock.

A deferral means your AME did not decide. The FAA instructs examiners that "If the requirements are not met, the AME must defer the exam and send the supporting documents to the FAA." Your application goes to the FAA for a decision. Your AME holds delegated authority to issue, renew and deny certificates under 14 CFR 67.407(b), and a deferral is that examiner declining to exercise it on the information in front of them.

A denial is a decision, and it carries a deadline. Under 14 CFR 67.409(a), a person denied a medical certificate by an AME may, "within 30 days after the date of the denial, apply in writing to the Federal Air Surgeon, Attention: Manager, Aeromedical Certification Division, AAM-300, Federal Aviation Administration, P.O. Box 25082, Oklahoma City, Oklahoma 73126, for reconsideration of that denial." The same paragraph adds the consequence of missing it: "If the person does not ask for reconsideration during the 30-day period after the date of the denial, he or she is considered to have withdrawn the application for a medical certificate."

A denial by an AME is also not the last word. Under 14 CFR 67.409(b)(1), denial by an aviation medical examiner "is not a denial by the Administrator under 49 U.S.C. 44703." Reconsideration authority sits with the Federal Air Surgeon, the Manager of the Aeromedical Certification Division, and each Regional Flight Surgeon (14 CFR 67.407(c)).

On timing, we will not give you a number. The FAA does not publish a guaranteed processing time for a deferred application, and any figure we printed here would be an estimate dressed up as a rule. What the regulation does fix is the 30-day reconsideration window after a denial, which is a deadline that runs against you rather than a wait that runs for you.

cardTitle: Motor vehicle actions - a separate 60-day report to the FAA
body:
A DUI or other alcohol- or drug-related driving incident creates a reporting obligation that is separate from your medical application. Under 14 CFR 61.15(e), "Each person holding a certificate issued under this part shall provide a written report of each motor vehicle action to the FAA, Civil Aviation Security Division (AMC-700), P.O. Box 25810, Oklahoma City, OK 73125, not later than 60 days after the motor vehicle action." The regulation specifies this mailing address. Check current FAA guidance for any additional accepted submission methods.

What counts as a "motor vehicle action" is broader than a conviction. 14 CFR 61.15(c) defines it to include a conviction for operating a motor vehicle while intoxicated by, impaired by, or under the influence of alcohol or a drug; the cancellation, suspension, or revocation of a license to operate a motor vehicle for such a cause; and the denial of an application for such a license for such a cause. An administrative action against your driving privileges can therefore be a reportable motor vehicle action even where there is no conviction.

The report must include your name, address, date of birth, and airman certificate number; the type of violation that resulted in the conviction or administrative action; its date; the State holding the record; and a statement of whether it arose from the same incident or the same factual circumstances as a previously reported motor vehicle action (14 CFR 61.15(e)(1) through (5)).

Under 14 CFR 61.15(f), failure to comply with the reporting requirement is itself grounds for denial of an application for up to 1 year, or for suspension or revocation of any certificate. Separately, under 14 CFR 61.15(d), a motor vehicle action occurring within 3 years of a previous one is grounds for the same.

14 CFR 61.15 also addresses drug offenses generally, and acts prohibited by 14 CFR 91.17(a) and 91.19(a). Those are grounds for denial, suspension, or revocation, but they do not carry the 60-day reporting requirement described above.

This is the certificate-side obligation. Your FAA medical application asks its own separate question about arrests, convictions, and administrative actions - see Item 18(v).

links.title: 14 CFR 61.15 - offenses involving alcohol or drugs

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, Item 46, BRAIN TUMOR (Intracranial Tumor) disposition table, All Classes (Updated 05/29/2024)

body:
The FAA publishes a disposition table for this condition: "BRAIN TUMOR (Intracranial Tumor)", All Classes (Updated 05/29/2024).

Every row of that table defers. For a benign brain tumor that was not surgically treated, for a benign brain tumor that was surgically treated or resected, and for a malignant (cancerous) brain tumor, the disposition the FAA gives the examiner is the same: "DEFER" and "Submit the information to the FAA for a possible Special Issuance."

The table sets a waiting period on two of those rows. For a benign tumor that was surgically treated or resected, it reads "After a two-year (2) recovery period, submit the following for FAA review:". For a malignant tumor it reads "After a five-year (5) recovery period following completion of chemotherapy, radiation, or surgery. (Maintenance biologic medication does not add to the above recovery time.)"

Every row asks for "A current, detailed neurological evaluation that meets FAA Specifications for Neurologic Evaluation generated from a clinic visit with the treating neurologist no more than 90 days before the AME exam." and "MRI brain performed no more than 12 months before the AME exam."

The table also routes two tumor types elsewhere: "If tumor type is Acoustic neuroma or Pituitary Tumor - see the corresponding section."

The table also names the testing and the submission format. On the surgically treated or resected row it asks for a "Neuropsychological (NP) evaluation that meets FAA Specifications for Neuropsychological Evaluations for Potential Neurocognitive Impairment. (Due to surgical resection, NP testing is required.)" On the untreated row that testing is conditional: "After review of the information submitted, a neuropsychological (NP) evaluation that meets FAA Specifications for Neuropsychological Evaluation for Potential Neurocognitive Impairment MAY be required."

For the imaging, the table states: "Submit both the report and a copy of the images on compact disc (CD) in DICOM readable format. (There MUST be a file name ‘DICOMDIR’ in the root directory of the CD-ROM)." It adds that a tumor "associated with a seizure" is also referred to the Seizure section, where "An additional recovery period may apply."

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, Item 40. Skin, Skin Cancer - All Classes disposition table

cardTitle: Basal cell and squamous cell skin cancer
body:
The FAA's "Skin Cancer - All Classes" disposition table covers basal cell cancer (BCC) and squamous cell cancer (SCC) separately from melanoma.

For the uncomplicated case the disposition is ISSUE, not deferral. The table's condition column reads "Basal cell cancer (BCC)", "Squamous cell cancer(SCC)", "Uncomplicated skin only. No organ involvement", and its disposition column reads "ISSUE", "Note BCC or SCC treated in block 60.", "If complicated lesion, see below."

The complicated case is different. For a "Complicated lesion" with "Metastatic lymph node or deep tissue involvement, aggressive pathology or other abnormalities", the disposition is "DEFER", "Submit reports to FAA for review." and "Follow-up certification - based on Special Issuance Authorization."

Where the pathology is not known, the table's disposition is "MORE INFO NEEDED".

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, Item 45. Lymphatics, Leukemia, Acute and Chronic disposition table

body:
The FAA's Item 45 disposition table has one row covering leukemia generally: "Leukemia, Acute and Chronic - All Types", for all classes, with the evaluation data "Submit a current status report and all pertinent medical reports" and the disposition "Requires FAA Decision".

Two kinds of leukemia are routed elsewhere by that same table. Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) and Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma (SLL) are sent to their own disposition table. Acute Lymphocytic Leukemia (ALL) has a separate FAA disposition table of its own, which the FAA publishes as a standalone document.

The Item 45 page also states the general rule its tables sit under: "Medical certificates must not be issued to an applicant with medical conditions that require deferral, or for any condition not listed that may result in sudden or subtle incapacitation without consulting the AMCD or the RFS." and "Medical documentation must be submitted for any condition in order to support an issuance of an airman medical certificate."

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners (Version 08/26/2026); Condition Not Listed disposition table, All Classes (Updated 03/25/2026)

body:
The FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners does not name thyroid cancer. A search of the Guide, including the complete Guide PDF (Version 08/26/2026), returns no page for it. The hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism tables address thyroid function, not thyroid cancer.

A condition the tables do not name falls to the FAA's "Condition Not Listed" table, All Classes (Updated 03/25/2026). That table tells the examiner: "When a diagnosis or condition is not listed in the disposition tables, the AME should assess whether the condition or its treatment could lead to sudden or subtle incapacitation."

It gives two outcomes. Where the "AME determines the individual is NOT at increased risk for sudden or subtle incapacitation", the disposition is "ISSUE" "and explain rationale in Item 60." Where the "AME determines the individual IS at increased risk for sudden or subtle incapacitation", the disposition is "DEFER".

The same table sets a limit on the examiner: "Medical certificates must not be issued to an individual with medical condition(s) that requires deferral, or for any condition not listed in the table that may result in sudden or subtle incapacitation without consulting the AMCD or the RFS."

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners (Version 08/26/2026); Condition Not Listed disposition table, All Classes (Updated 03/25/2026)

body:
The FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners does not name multiple myeloma. A search of the Guide, including the complete Guide PDF (Version 08/26/2026), returns no page for multiple myeloma, plasmacytoma or monoclonal gammopathy.

The FAA does not state which of its tables applies, and this app does not choose one for you.

A condition the tables do not name falls to the FAA's "Condition Not Listed" table, All Classes (Updated 03/25/2026). That table states: "When a diagnosis or condition is not listed in the disposition tables, the AME should assess whether the condition or its treatment could lead to sudden or subtle incapacitation."

It also states: "Medical certificates must not be issued to an individual with medical condition(s) that requires deferral, or for any condition not listed in the table that may result in sudden or subtle incapacitation without consulting the AMCD or the RFS."
